utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with some administrative matters first. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we've had notice that the plenary will now take place on the 12th and the 13th of December, two of the original days which were fixed. It will not take place on the 11th, and therefore we shall sit that day, having in mind the time that's been lost. We will sit, of course, on the 18th, where we said we would have administrative matters. It may be that, if we get that far, there may be some evidence to be finished up, and closer to the time, we'll decide whether we'll sit that afternoon or not, but the parties should have that time available for sitting, if necessary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already described the pattern of attacks that you saw occurring, and you have described the military formation present in particular regions, and I would like to discuss with you now what you can tell us about crimes occurring in particular places named in the indictment. The first place I would like to turn to is the Kostajnica region, in particular, the regions Dubica, Cerovljani, and Bacin. On Friday you testified that fighting took place in this region until September 1991, and you also testified at an earlier point in time that you observed the fighting personally from the Bosnia side of the river. You also mentioned already that you travelled through the region in November 1991, on your way to Petrinja, and that you saw the Croatian villages or parts of villages where Croats had lived, that they were destroyed and the population gone. You also already mentioned a military headquarters in Samarica, and my question to you is: What kind of a facility was it? Was it -- of what structure was it the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Samarica was the headquarters of the operative group for the JNA for Banija and Kordun, and this headquarters was the military command for the area. The 7th Banija Division had its headquarters up there as well, as did the special police units, or rather -- well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we actually had managed to produce charts of the military formations on the ground at that time, and with the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness these charts now. And it has three pages: one showing the TO structure, one showing the JNA operational group that the witness just mentioned, and the third is actually a map that is just showing you where the various places are located.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, if you look at the first chart. And I have to read it to you because it's in English language. It says: "Croatian operative zones of the TO SAO Krajina," and it simply shows the command structure, with the Prime Minister on top; the Main Staff of the TO, with first General Djujic, and then, of course, you have already said that changed; and then you have here the three operational zones: the first one for Dalmatia and Lika, the second one Slunj, and the third one Kostajnica, Petrinja, Sisak. Is that correct? Is the chart correct in relation to the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath Slunj you should add Vojnic and Vrginmost. And underneath Petrinja, what should be added is Glina and Dvor na Uni. Otherwise, the rest is as it was here, was as it was in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And if you look at the second page, you have the JNA Operation Group Banija-Kordun-Lika after October 1991, and it shows here already the headquarters Samarica and its commander Jasan Maric. Then you have the various sections, that is the 2nd and 3rd Operative Zone of the TO with Colonel Vujaklija, JNA 5th Military District Units, then the 6th Lika Division, the Loznica Brigade from Serbia that you mentioned, and the Special Police Units Krajina, and then you also have here the Banija Division attached to the TO, and the unspecified JNA units attached to the 5th Military District. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Operative Group Banija Kordun" here and "Lika." The commander was General Spiro Nikovic in the month of November. I don't know the dates, from when until when.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then I'm not sure whether Lika was under this Operative Group or whether it had its own command, the 6th Lika Division. But anyway, so there, that's what it was like. This is what it was like. And underneath the Loznica Brigade you should add the Sabac Brigade from Serbia and the Vojvodina Brigade from Serbia as well, and a paratrooper unit from Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The paratroop from Nis, did it have a particular -- did it have a particular name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a special paratroop unit. I don't know what the name was exactly, whether that was its name or whether it had another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we put it on the overhead projector? Yes. Yes. Thank you. And the third, the third page. Can you please turn it around to the map. The third page. Can you please put the third page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually a map showing the 5th Military District region, the Naval Military District region, and the places that we actually spoke about so far. Looking at it, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border between the Naval Military District and the 5th Military District was here, this line. Lika belonged to the 5th Military District, and Northern Dalmatia to the Naval Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's described as tab 120, this exhibit. Which exhibit is that in?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 120 was actually the creation of the Operational Zones and their composition with the three military districts. But this would now, of course, need to have a different exhibit number because it's an entirely new exhibit. It's just a reference to the document that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Give it a new number, please, the next number. It's being suggested that we have tab 171 of 352. It probably makes very little difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you had mentioned the 7th Banija Division and that Mr. Bogdan Vajagic commanded it up to September 1991. Do you know who commanded it in October, November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Vajagic was his name, and the division was reformed, restructured as a formation of the Territorial Defence, but it remained the same in content.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that Special Police Units were also there, so the units attached to the parallel structure. In -- in October, end of October, and November 1991, who in person was there from the parallel structure? Which commanding person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Borojevic, and he was the commander of that Special Police Unit. His name was Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were volunteer units or paramilitary units as well in that region in Kostajnica attached to the Samarica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you visit the headquarters in Samarica personally, and if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-November 1991, while I was in Petrinja, I was invited by General Spiro Nikovic to go to Samarica to visit him, but I never went there, for security reasons. I wasn't quite sure what was happening up there and what existed up there, because people had been telling me that there were different units stationed there, that there were killings that had taken place and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you fear for your own safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These units that you mentioned, these people that were stationed there, were they opposing your politics, or why would you fear for your own safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a constant conflict between the parallel structures there: the state security, the DB, and the police force, and part of the SDS, the regional board of the SDS. So there was a political conflict. But the SDS, the regional board of the SDS, supported me and criticised those parallel structures, especially the police force of Krajina and Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if the witness could point the location of Samarica in this third tab in this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you heard Their Honours asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Samarica is a hill which is located where the Bosanski Novi -- or rather, Dvor na Uni, Kostajnica, and Petrinja municipalities meet, which means here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing, actually, at the word "Banija," in the region of the word "Banija." This map is not specific enough to show the place itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it near from Petrinja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's between Kostajnica and Petrinja, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in the region in November, did you see the villages Dubica, Cerovljani, and Bacin; and if so, what did they look like in relation to the destruction that ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those villages were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there churches in these villages and were they destroyed as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I arrived in Kostajnica from the Petrinja direction, and I saw those villages afterwards, later on, and they had been completely destroyed and without any inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The villagers, or the people living, the Croat people living in these villages, had they posed a threat to the Serbs in the region in October/November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had not. The fighting was over by mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned already you heard of killings. Did you get information that 120 Croatian villagers from these three villages had been killed in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive information to that effect. My information was different, in 1994/1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was your information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from people from Dubica that they had taken revenge in Bacin for what had happened in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to now move on to the region Korenica, Ogulin, and in particular, the villages Saborsko, Poljanak, and Lipovanic. You have already mentioned the training ground in Slunj and the officer Cedomir Bulat being in charge there. Do you know which JNA corps were active in this region end of November until mid - sorry - end of October until mid-November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command was active there, the command from Plitvice, that is, Mukinje, and from the training ground. I had information that this was the operative zone of the 6th Lika Division and units within it, or in coordination -- acting in coordination with it or subordinated to it. I also heard that there was an advance command position of the Rijeka Corps, and that the Vojvodina Brigade was active there for a while, as well as members of the paratroop units from Nis, and the Territorial Defence from the area. Who was exactly the highest commanding officer or command, I don't know. According to establishment, if there was a forward command post the Rijeka Corps, then they must have had the highest-ranking officer within it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, was there also the 1st Partisan Light Brigade in this region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Partisan Light Brigade was within the territory of the municipality of Gracac and a part of the municipality of Gospic, in the southern part of Lika, not around Plitvice. Up there, I think it was the 5th Brigade that was active.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I would briefly talk -- I would like to briefly talk to you about this 1st Partisan Light Brigade. Who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Petar Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a JNA officer, dispatched from the General Staff in September 1991 to form the 1st Light Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the -- I would like to have closed session very briefly, for two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually meet Colonel Trbojevic, and what dealings did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least on two occasions. The first time, when he came from Belgrade, I was called to the command of the Knin Corps by General Vukovic, and he introduced me to Colonel Trbojevic. And he said that Colonel Trbojevic was going to be the commander of the 1st Light Partisan Brigade and that men would not respond to the mobilisation because of its name, so that I should appeal to them to sign up, and that was the reason why I met with Colonel Trbojevic. I said to General Vukovic that I would do that if it was going to be called a brigade of the Territorial Defence, and he said, "Okay, then." And indeed, later on, in communication with us, it was referred to as the 1st TO Brigade, but in reality it was known as the 1st Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean this brigade cooperated with the Knin Corps? Because you mentioned Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the tab 161 and 162 of Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do we need to be in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the two documents, are they related to the mobilisation that you just mentioned to us, that is, a mobilisation order of the 26th of October, 1991, and the other one also a mobilisation order of that same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the first document, there is a reference made to a mobilisation issued by the SFRY Presidency of the 4th of October, 1991. Was that the reason why this mobilisation was actually ordered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document refers to that, and this other one as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That should be enough. We don't need to discuss more details on this matter. In relation to the region of Plitvice and the villages Saborsko, Poljanak, and Lipovanic, did the Korenica municipal TO staff cover that same region, and if so, who was the commander there in October, November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Staff of the TO Korenica did cover it, but the surrounding Serbian areas had been linked to the Korenica municipality. And the commander of the Municipal Staff was Colonel Milos Cvijeticanin, or Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he an active JNA officer; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been an active officer in Zadar prior to that, and he probably continued to be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was personnel of the DB Serbia in that region active in this region; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After August 1991, a base of the DB of Serbia was in Korenica or, rather, Frenki's base was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that Frenki himself was there, or who was there in charge of this section?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that those men from the DB were there. And I personally had met Frenki there earlier, on earlier occasions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You already mentioned the parachute units from Nis, and does -- do they have special uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore red berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to go into closed session for two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said they were also there in October/November 1991. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there until February 1992. From when exactly, I can't say, but they were there during combat activities. I know because I was in the SIT factory near Udbina in 1992 when the municipality of Udbina was being established, and Colonel Milivojevic was in the staff, and he was in command in the area. A member of the parachute unit came to the headquarters wearing combat gear with gloves without fingers. He shook hands with me, and he gave me as a gift a red beret, his red beret, the kind that he wore. But he told me not to put it on my head because it was worn only by men who had sworn to fight to the death. I took the beret and I hid it in the corner of my cupboard so the children wouldn't play with it because I thought it was damned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person that spoke to you from the parachute unit, did he tell you where he had been fighting? Did he mention anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the region around Vrhovine. I don't know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Open session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In October/November 1991, were the villages Saborsko, Poljanak, and Lipovanic surrounded by Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did these villages at that time pose a threat to the Serbs in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When -- do you know when these villages were attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting there around the 17th of November or mid-November in 1991. So mid-November there was combat around Slunj, and that is the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you get the information that end of October until the 12th of November, Croat civilians were killed in these three villages? Do you know anything of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like -- did you hear it later on? Did you get any information later on about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I saw - that is in 1994 - that the villages had been destroyed and that they were abandoned, that there were no inhabitants in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to move to the third region, that is Northern Dalmatia with Skabrnje, Nadin, and Bruska, and particularly the time period November 1991 to February 1992. These villages that I just mentioned, are they all in the Benkovac municipality or the Serbian -- the so-called Serbian Zadar region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Benkovac municipality at that time, November 1991 to February 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he related to Frenki, Martic, and the others of the parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a Crisis Staff in Benkovac? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Crisis Staff in Benkovac which was a body that was not envisaged by the documents of the municipality but was formed on the initiative of the local authorities in Benkovac itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the Martic police involved in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were representatives, that is of the civilian authorities, the police, the TO; therefore, all the structures that existed within the municipality of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the JNA involved in this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Captain Dragan had a training facility in the Benkovac region. Was he there in November 1991? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Frenki, was he also in this region in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Frenki was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the Martic police in the region in November 1991, do you know who was in charge of them there in this particular region of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the regular police and the special police. The head of the special police was Goran Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware that Skabrnja and Nadin were attacked in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some fighting there, but I don't know exactly the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness two exhibits. The first is tab 164 of Exhibit 352, and the other one is tab 75 of that same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the first one, it is actually a note about fighting concerning the Yugoslav army and Martic in the villages -- in the Croatian villages in Benkovac municipality of September 1991. Witness, this is a document compiled by the Croatian authorities, and looking -- looking at it, on the second page there is a quote, and I quote on the second page: "In accordance with Colonel Mladic's orders, Martic's terrorists, together with military reservists, are entering all houses by force, robbing and taking everything they need and destroying the rest." And my question is: Did that happen in that region as indicated here in this note? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I have here the second document. It is a report of the SAO Krajina headquarters of the 17th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous one, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is the first document? Is it tab 165? 164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get this right. It's 164, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it is actually a document provided by the Croatian authorities, and I just wanted to address the contents of this document with the witness, whether such attacks as described here, with robbing and destroying, took place in the region. That was the purpose of putting it to the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next document, tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, it's a report of the SAO Krajina headquarters of the 17th of September, 1991. And if you look at the seal and the header, is that a -- are they authentic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what position did this person Maglov, Petar have? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this document, there is the mentioning of the TO Benkovac staff on the first page and an order given by Milan Martic. And as point 2, there is mentioned: "Have an armoured train go from Kosovo station to near Tepljuh and open heavy fire on the region of Siveric." What kind of an armoured train was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an armoured train that Frenki made in Strmica, a combat armoured train.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was in charge of this train? Do you know who commanded the conduct of this train?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guska was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To whom was he related? Was he part of this parallel structure? Who was he subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki and Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the villages Skabrnja and Nadin, did they pose a threat to the Serbs in the region, or the JNA, in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Serbs, no; but in a sense, they jeopardised the flank of the JNA forces in the region of Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which way did they jeopardise the flank of the JNA units? Was the Croatian army in these villages in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I just know that General Vukovic said that before the winter he had to level the lines where his units had been deployed in that region, to even them out. I said General Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please, for one question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, to whom did General Vukovic say that, and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that in his office, at the headquarters of the 9th Corps in Knin. Actually, he invited me and asked me to point to the Northern Dalmatian region on the map and indicate the Serbian settlements in that area, that is, from Sibenik towards Zadar, the municipalities of Knin, Sibenik, Benkovac. And I pointed them out to him. In the area of Benkovac, it's not really possible to indicate with precision because the population is mixed to quite a considerable degree. And such compact areas of Serbian and Croatian settlements are distributed in the form of a curve, so that as I pointed them out, this was in a curving position. And then he waved his head and said, "I can't leave it like that until the winter. I have to make the lines straight." That's what he said, that he had to deploy his unit in a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the villages Skabrnja and Nadin disturbing the straight line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a sense. In relation to that line, they were indented. The area of Zemunik and towards Zadar, where the 9th Corps units were deployed, they formed a kind of wedge, and Skabrnja was inside it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go to open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know when these villages, Skabrnja and Nadin, were attacked and which -- in which way, which forces took part in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt later -- I wasn't fully informed at the time. I was later informed that these were Skabrnja and Nadin, in November 1991. JNA units took part, as well as units that were coordinated by the Crisis Staff in Benkovac, which means the TO and the police and all armed formations that were in the area of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you get information that Croatian civilians were murdered during the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt later that they had been.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who informed you, and what did this person tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. He said that they went there to straighten out the region, to straighten out the lines in Skabrnja. And he said that Goran Opacic had also taken part in the attack, or rather, at the beginning of the attack, but afterwards that he had left. He told me that for personal reasons, because Goran Opacic, in June 1992, mistreated me in person, and that is probably what prompted [redacted]to mention him specifically to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean Goran Opacic mistreated you in person, or this [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Goran Opacic mistreated me. He mistreated me and some other people from the Regional Board of the SDS of Krajina in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did he -- what was the occasion that he mistreated you, and what did he actually do to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, 1992, after, in Djevrske -- no, in Bratiskovci. I beg your pardon. That's a village which was joined from the Sibenik municipality to the Knin municipality. And he said that Slobodan Milosevic was not to be trusted, believed. And when at that meeting I tried to prove to the people what he wanted to give to Croatia in March 1991, that means when I was talking about Bihac and the road from Benkovac to Drnis, so two days after that, or three days later, Goran Opacic and his men waited for me in Benkovac and wanted to liquidate me physically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me clarify something. Who said that Slobodan Milosevic was not to be trusted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I said that to the people at the meeting in Bratiskovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person Goran Opacic that you mentioned, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Klempo was what they called him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he close to Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, close, intimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to move on to Bruska. You have already mentioned Bruska and how you visited it. In December 1991, was there any fighting in or around the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware that ten civilians were killed in the village of Bruska on the 21st of December, 1991, and how it came about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about that, later on. And how it came about was that Goran Opacic, with a few of his men, threw a bomb into the house where the inhabitants were sitting. And Croats were killed, the Croats who were there, and a Serb postman who was sitting there with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Closed session, please, for one question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who informed you about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did he inform you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years ago, a year and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian villagers return to the region of Skabrnja or Bruska before Operation Storm? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, with the help of the usher, I would like to put to you Exhibit -- tab 166 of Exhibit 352. And there is a document of the Ministry of Internal Affairs dated the 28th of September, 1992, signed and stamped. Can you first of all comment on the header and the stamp and the signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which corresponds to the contents, but the signature is not that of Martic. Somebody signed for him, probably someone from the command of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the stamp, is it the stamp that was used at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this document, there is a reference made to -- I quote: "We have the --" I can't read that word. Sorry. Mine was not readable. "We have the surely information that during the 29/30-1992 by force immigration of the population is planned for Skabrnja, Novigrad, and Pridraga." And a little bit further down: "... we inform you that we will be forced to prevent by force arrival of -- on the territory of RSK." Do you know that anything happened at that time, in September 1992, in relation to the return of the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that people talked about it and that it was the position by the people in the government that the Croats should not be allowed to return. I don't know exactly, in any precise terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's enough for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, who interpreted, translated this document? I'm interested in the form of the document. Was it faxed?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is actually a UN -- we received this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document from the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: UNPROFOR. And I'm actually -- I'm not sure who translated it. I assume they, not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could tell us what the previous documents, the handwritten documents, are which were put before this document under the same tab number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is just a memo from UNPROFOR related to the situation at that time, and attached was this statement from Martic, Martic's ministry. The other questions I can't actually answer. It is a letter written to UNPROFOR and the State Committee for Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we have -- you have already mentioned Dubrovnik and the fighting in Dubrovnik and what the goal was in relation to this region. Did the Bosnian Serbs have a particular goal for the region around Dubrovnik? Did you ever have a conversation related to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. It was their target that the Republika Srpska should come out onto the sea to the south of Dubrovnik, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you have conversation of that kind or did you hear them quote such things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from Biljana Plavsic, that Republika Srpska should be given an outlet to the sea at the rocks of Konavle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did she say that? Did she say that publicly and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she said that publicly in 1994 or 1995. I'm not quite sure now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- when we spoke about the intercepts in relation to the Martic arrest, there was actually one intercept that I did not put to the witness, and I would like to do that just now, and it is -- it's tab 37 of the intercept binder 353.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you listen to an intercepted conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How familiar are you with Mr. Krajisnik's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the voice well. I heard him on several occasions. He uses the Sarajevo dialect with his own personal type of intonation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I do not like to go into any details. It's not necessity point in time. Thank you. Witness, we have seen from several documents that you had actually put -- discussed and explained to us that civilian and military courts were established in the SAO Krajina and the RSK, and we also have seen the request of the RSK to the VJ to transfer staff for military courts. Does that mean that civil and military courts did function in the years 1991 to 1995 in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware whether any war crimes committed against the non-Serbs, the non-Serbs in the region, were investigated by the judiciary and led to a result such as a conviction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for one group from Drvenik for a crime in Rupe or thereabouts. In 1993, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of group -- what kind of group was it? Who was convicted of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group belonging to the army of the Srpska Krajina from Drvenik where it had killed some civilians. This was around the village of Rupe or around that area, and they were arrested and taken to trial. I don't know what the outcome of the trial was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The victims of these crimes, what ethnicity did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already described the looting that took place after attacks on --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I do apologise. Or one of them was perhaps killed at Rupe, and they killed some Croats from their own village. Perhaps that was it. Perhaps that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already described the looting that took place after attacks on Croatian villages, and I would like to ask you a question now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever have -- did you ever speak or have a conversation with Branko Kostic, the member of the SFRY Presidency, concerning looting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On the 31st of December, 1991, on the premises of the Presidency of Yugoslavia in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you talk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while we were waiting for Borisav Jovic to arrive, he was saying -- he was telling us a joke, and he asked me whether I knew what a Montenegrin flak jacket was. And then he explained to me that actually they were prosciutto hams placed one in front and one behind. And he showed his chest and his back and said that the Montenegrins wore these prosciutto hams as flak jackets. And then he went on to comment and said that the Montenegrin reservists in the Konavle region liked shooting prosciutto hams mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already described the two detention facilities in Knin, and I just need a few more details on this. Were Croats detained in a part of the old Knin hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This old Knin hospital, where was it situated in Knin in relation to the government buildings and the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the headquarters of the 9th Corps and the government building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean they were close?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who ran the detention facility, and in which time period did it function as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police were at the head, and it functioned as a prison for a long time. I don't know when it started being used in that way, but sometime in the middle of the summer of 1991 until the end of 1992. And later on, when the prison was taken over by the Ministry of Justice and when Ilija Tauz came and brought in professional prison guards, it was moved to the other wing of the old hospital, and that's where the prison was later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many -- what kind of people were kept there; civilians, combatants, men, women? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian police force and army who had been taken prisoner. And later on, I heard that there were some civilians too, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many Croats were detained there at a given time? What was the capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the capacity was. Well, tens, dozens.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know how long the detainees were kept there? I mean, over which time period were they kept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was in 1991 at any rate. The autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I mean the individual detainees, how were they kept there, the time period; just for a few days or months? The individual detainees, how long would they be detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly. There were some exchanges that took place. Some of them were exchanged and, therefore, released.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that detainees -- it was known that detainees were mistreated there. Who mistreated them and in which way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards who were policemen. I heard later on that they even brought in citizens from the streets to mistreat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "citizens from the streets," which ethnicity had the victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that some were exchanged, and my question is: Were you actually involved in some of these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of September 1991, when Ambassador Wijnaendts arrived after the signing of my statement and the accepting observers from the European Community, he suggested that as an act of good faith and goodwill that he could take off a group of Croats, prisoners, with him in the helicopters. And I called upon Nikola Amanovic from the police force and asked him whether we could meet that request made by Ambassador Wijnaendts. And Amanovic arrived and he brought a list of prisoners with him, detainees who were in prison, and I handed the list over to Ambassador Wijnaendts. This was in front of the Knin Assembly building. So it was all standing on our feet outside. The Ambassador took a pen and drew some circles round some names on the list, as many as he could take with him. And that's what happened on that occasion. That was my participation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many people were listed on the list, and what kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that they were Croatian policemen or guardsmen who were the prisoners. And there was another instance, one or two cases, in fact, in July, August - I don't remember exactly when - but on that occasion, General Niko Spirovic -- I beg your pardon, Spiro Nikovic is his name, he called me to ask Martic to let a Croatian policeman out of prison, to release him, because the Croatian police force from Sibenik had requested this. And also on another occasion received another message from Zadar via the head of -- from a doctor in Sibenik and a relation of mine whether I could do anything to ensure the release of a policeman from Zadar who was being held in a prison in Knin. So those were the cases that I personally know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 168 of Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Is this related to one of the releases that you just mentioned? It's an order dated the 25th of July, 1991, in relation to the release of Osman Vikic from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at the name, is that a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the name, I would say he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you need [Realtime transcript read in error: "do you know"] a Prime Minister's signature in order to release a prisoner? Was it common at that time? I said "do you need" not "do you know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But for some reason the Prime Minister was asked to sign as justification to have this person released. I don't know why. But it was Minister Martic, in public, once who made a comment that this was a mistake that had been done through the Prime Minister and General Nikovic and that he was sorry that this had actually taken place, and this was published in the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have to stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the events in 1991, you were in a leading political position in the SAO Krajina, and you were also the head of the TO, and you told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The senior legal officer, please. Just a moment. Just go on. It's totally different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said from 1991 onwards when the JNA was involved, you saw what was happening to the Croatian population. How did this make you feel at that time? How did you feel about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I felt that this didn't bode well for the Serbs either, that it was bad and that it compromised all the political principles for which the Serbs in Krajina had fought for until that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were a kind of a spokesman of the Krajina, and we even saw you mentioned in one article as the chancellor of Krajina. And you also said that you were backed, and the people listened to you. Why did you not oppose more vehemently what was going on, and why did you continue to have the functions that you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I became exclusively interested in the fate of my people. I became an ethnoegotist, if I can put it that way - selfish - and I took care of only my own people and forgot the others. And I sort of saw my political role in that light. I liked performing this role, and I would tell the public what people expected me to say. So I had entered this vicious circle from which it was difficult to extricate myself. And I did think that ultimately, after the war, a solution would be found and that things could be settled politically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are actually the questions that the Prosecution has to this witness. I'm actually finished, faster than I expected it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you repeat the final comment in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which one do you mean? Oh, you mean that we are finished with our questions. Yes. The Prosecution has now finished its questions that we're to put to the witness, and faster as expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient time. We'll go to cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic, after the break. Twenty minutes.

utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have been given the testimony of this witness on tapes, and I would like at the beginning to play one of those many videotapes, the first one. The first one will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let us see what -- let us just see what this is. This is tapes of his interview, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A part of the first tape of his conversations with the lady opposite and with the investigator, upon which I could put some questions to the witness and ask him to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the track has been identified. It will have to be in private session, as the registrar points out, because of the facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the video be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] ... the year 1991, and in connection with that, I would like to say the following. You see it was really that I was reacting on a daily basis, day in and day out I reacted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. every day to events, external events and in order to represent the interests of the Serbs in Krajina, the people I represented. And in all my interventions, what I wished was really one thing. That where Serbs in Croatia and primarily in Krajina, that I ensure a just, a harmonious relationship in Croatia, relations in Croatia. And in no way wore murder and suffering. In that sense, I also issued some statements. One was, for example, also taken up and published in the press, it was a statement of the 21st of August, 1991. And it referred to the attempt to preserve peace in the area of Kijevo. I already talked about that. And another statement, which I made, I gave on the 29th of August, 1991, that was also published by the press. And in this statement I said that we do not wish bloodshed between Serbs, Serbian and Croat population. And that we wouldn't wish to take over, to subjugate a single village, Croatian village, and not to occupy a single particle of Croatian territory, nor to do any harm to the Croatian nation. And then at the end something that I believe I already mentioned earlier with the international representative Mr. Galbraith, I agreed with this international proposal which was submitted for the status of Krajina within Croatia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes on. These are just excerpts from the tape and it's longer than this, and I would like to ask my questions once we've seen all of it. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And now if you will allow me, another two sentences to devote it to another topic, to devote them to another topic. And it concerns that document which was already on this table, which has been on this table. It is the official document number 63. It is a document of an audit to the third operation cell, to the command of the third operation cell. I already talked that, and in connection with that, I would like to in this context, I would like to add the following -- "MR. HARDIN: Just let me just interrupt, for reference purposes, that's the document that is marked MBW863. Yes now, just one second, yes, it's all right now. The ERN number is 0207 -- 7 -- 794 – 948/unclear just made a copy/unclear. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And I would like to say the following, concerning that document. It is certain that I signed that document, but it is also certain that if I hadn't signed it, somebody else would have signed it. Well, I have been asking myself and I wonder why that has been slipped to me and that I then signed it. I'd like to be clear about that. It is again the work of that Milosevic parallel structure operating in Krajina. In that way, they certainly wanted to compromise me. To compromise me vis-a-vis the legitimate representatives of the Croatian authorities, in the attempt to resolve the open issues in a peaceful manner. To present me as a liar and to present me as somebody who is for war and not for peace. And in that situation at the time, it was the work for compromising me, it was done in order to compromise me and to present me as a person who is not for peace and not for the Vance's plan. And it seems to me that this document is still carrying, is still having this function of compromising me, even today at this very moment. And I feel that it is compromising me even today. It is placing me in a different light, and also me, and the intentions, and my real intentions, what they were. And that was to resolve the political problems without violence, and to enable and ensure the coexistence of the Serbian and Croatian people without a conflict. And this is what --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "MR. HARDIN: OK. Mr. Babic, let me just ask you a question in point about what you just said a few minutes ago. You said that on the 29th of August 1991, in essence you didn't wish bloodshed, and I don't recall what else you said, but it was that/unclear. And I have a representation of what is an article from Politika, dated 29th of August 1991. I think that this is just a summary of the article, but what I have written here is: 'Milan Babic states that the southern parts of the SAO Krajina are almost entirely under control of armed people, after the SAO Krajina forces liberated Kijevo, Vrliku, Otisic, and other areas. He adds that no forces from the Republic of Serbia participated in the operation and that the Serbs shall shrink from no means to defend their right to independence.' And then it goes on to state: 'Krajina,' he states: 'cannot remain within Croatia, even if Croatia remained in Yugoslavia.' Do you recall that interview? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] No. As I remember it, how my statement went that we have no claims towards Croatia or the Croatian people. "MR. HARDIN: In the press summary that you mentioned when you were talking, is this the one, the same interview that we're talking about? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, I found this. I got it from a friend of mine. He reminded me of this. But we can check with the press and check it then. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Do you want to give this to us, what you have there? "MR. MUELLER: Is this the article or is it not? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] No it is not the article."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Mr. Babic, I did not understand actually what you meant when you said that my plan was, as a regional politician, was to come to an agreement with the Croatians within the framework of Croatia. From when onwards did you have this plan? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, I could say it was my plan or my intention to do it, it was from the beginning of September 1990. It was when, with Jerko, Jerko Vukas, the mayor of Sinj, when we agreed for a meeting with the representatives of the Croatian government and of the Croatian parliament. On the 10th of September, we signed an agreement. In the documents, I submitted a copy of this agreement where we stated we agreed that all open questions will be resolved through the institution. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yeah, let's not go into details, and get not let -- let's not get distracted by details. You say since September 1990 you wanted to solve the problem with Croatia. Why, then, did you pass so many decisions annexing the SAO Krajina to Serbia, to Yugoslavia? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, I said that these were the day-to-day reactions to these external events. Concerning some of these events have already been discussed here. I also mentioned a number of times that this parallel structure was being set up in Krajina, which had an impact on the external events. They took over, they had the monopoly over the organs of force, through the institution of the police, the state security. And then also the -- the public was being threatened. They were -- I mentioned a number of times also this film which was being shown on television concerning Martin Spegelj and the purported attack on Knin. And we -- we were -- this -- we considered that we were being publicly -- it was a kind of a public threat to us, and this -- us, as well as the public at large. And we also -- we wanted to get Milosevic to take a clear stand; namely, we wanted to provoke him and not to manipulate the public with false hopes, through false hopes. And that is why I mentioned that these reactions, we had these reactions to these day-to-day events. And after this atmosphere of fear was created, and after the armed conflicts were being -- occurred, the next opportunity for resolving our status came at the international conference. And then again similar means were used by Milosevic and his people. "In front of the apartment of Borivoj Rasuo at the beginning -- at the beginning of The Hague conference there was a big -- in big letters what I read, big, it was written in red, `Babic, traitor.' And Rasuo -- Rasuo said that this was written by a policeman who lived next to him. "I already mentioned how Frenki in the police station in Knin, before I went to the first preparatory meeting in Paris for The Hague Conference, that he was inciting people against me by saying that I was a traitor and so. Then at the time, Slobodan Milosevic; then Simovic; (redacted), I won't list all the others, but however, many people from Serbia and from the -- among -- from the ranks of the authorities were -- were creating this climate among the population and generating thus expectations among the people living in Krajina and that it is their natural right to remain in Yugoslavia and that they will have to make another -- choose an option. "I mentioned to you that this -- at a certain point I couldn't take this atmosphere, this pressure, any more, and I didn't go to Paris to this preparatory meeting. I was really pressed on the one side by the public opinion and authorities in Serbia, and on the other hand, this pressure that I'm a traitor of the Serbian nation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any more, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] So I'm -- I'm describing to you this atmosphere which prevailed at the time, and how -- how we acted as rational politicians. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Mr. Babic, I still don't understand your position in relation to what your plans were. You say in September 1990, your plan was actually -- or you intended to solve the problems internally in Croatia. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yes. Please. And then comes this period where clashes occur and when conflict comes up, and then you -- do I understand that you still continued to have this plan or did you give it up for a while? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] That was in my head and in my heart, but not always in my mouth. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yes. And in autumn 1991, you again wanted to discuss and negotiate with the Croats. Is that what you say? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, an opportunity occurred for that. It was with -- through the mediation of the international community. I already mentioned what these relations were, how they -- how they progressed, and maybe it was my mistake not to have sufficient courage to take this step publicly. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But did you -- "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, these were my weaknesses. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But no, let's not speak about your weaknesses now. Did you --" "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: We are talking about 1991 now."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] But what I wanted to say was that Tudjman did not want to have a public meeting, a meeting that would be public, made public. You see, he offered that this meeting take place. I accepted but that it had to be made known public. But I received no feedback on this. So we then also proposed this constitutional solution where the Krajina would be within the framework of Croatia as a region, Krajina region, district. And that's why they called me the district leader, the head, the `Zupan.' Even Biljana Plavsic called me leader of the district, namely, the person who wants the Krajina to be a district, a region of Croatia. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But, Mr. Babic, it's very difficult when you jump between the years. If I understand you now correctly, it's in 1990 you were strongly moving to having an Autonomous Region Krajina within Croatia. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. And formally it was, up to the end of May 1991. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But then you gave it up and never pursued it. Isn't that -- isn't that the fact? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, you see, there was no possibility for pursuing, for opening this matter. I was really limited by the circumstances which were being created around us, and Croatia was publicly saying that Serbia is abusing of Krajina for its public purposes, ends. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yeah. Isn't that --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But you, at the moment, you've just said he created parallel structure in the Krajina. He undermined my plan. That is what you said, but you did not explain what you mean. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. And I'm convinced of that. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yes. But I don't really understand that. How could -- how could he do that? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] How could he? "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yeah."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just suspend matters for a moment, please. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just able to find the -- the script, the script from the interview, and I just noticed that in this tape that is just now played to us, two sentences are actually dropped. They are cut out. And I think it, in a certain way, changes what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What are the two sentences?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After: "And Croatia was publicly stating that Serbia is abusing of Krajina for its public purposes, ends." And then I asked the witness: "Yes. Isn't that the truth?" And the witness answered: "Yes, but what I want to say is how Milosevic and others abused Krajina, individual persons and its institutions." This is what the witness said, and this is actually left out, this short quote. From the rest -- before is played and the after is played, but this is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In due course this extract will have to be exhibited. You will have, of course, the opportunity to check that it's correct and it has been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There were also other breaks, and I have only now found it in this huge transcript, and we'll check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. Yes. Let's go on with the playing, please. One at a time. One at a time. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic. Yes. What is it, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to draw your attention simply to one matter. I agree that we should assess everything when we see it in full context, but for several days, we've been listening to the intercepts, and excerpts taken from those, just two sentences. So if this principle refers to the substance, that is to say that every document and every transcript should be viewed in its entirety, I agree that it be so. However, the remark I have to make -- the remark made by the Prosecution about the two sentences I think is not justified, because when we listen to the intercepts, quite a different method was applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. We will have the full extracts exhibited. Then we shall be able to see for ourselves what it in fact says. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These shortenings were for the economy of time, because the points upon which the lady opposite is insisting upon isn't lost. He did say it. But it was cut out -- what she was saying is cut out, which is not as essential for the witness statement. But the shortenings and abridging that was made was because they were your tapes and not my own. So there was no intention to skip over anything, just to see the manner in which this witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When the extracts are finished, the tape as it has been played will be exhibited. No doubt it will have to be done under seal. And then we will exhibit also the transcript. But this whole matter must be kept within bounds. Yes, Mr. Mueller. Then we really must get on with the playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Just for the sake of fairness and safeguarding the rights of my client as a witness who is supposed to tell here the truth, if anything else then the truth, I consider that he should at least be given a notice that he is now listening to excerpts of a tape, which was not done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he's just heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: He heard it after. He heard it after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not waste further time. There is no unfairness so far. Yes. One other matter. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, can you tell us which -- the document that was referred to, an order of the -- to the 3rd Operative Zone signed by the witness. Is that an exhibit of ours or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There -- the first document was actually a -- tab 143 of Exhibit 352, and it refers to this command structure in the 3rd Operational Zone. But the very first document that Mr. Milosevic actually -- that is mentioned in the interview is a document not exhibited Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by us, and if Mr. Milosevic wants to refer to it, it would have to become a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But it was the order which I specifically asked about. That's tab 142, Exhibit 352. Yes. Now, let's go back to the playing, if we may, of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that I was mentioning something. I am not mentioning anything. I'm just showing what the witness was saying. I have not said anything so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What counsel said was that if you want the statement exhibited - it was referred to in the tape - if you want it exhibited, you can ask and it can be a new exhibit number. Let us go on with the playing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] ... September 1990. And we stabilised the situation in the area of Knin, and after a period of lack of stability, and when we also made these also statements concerning peace, pacifying, and undertook certain activities, two things emerged. "At first what emerged was this Council of National Resistance against the subjugation of Serbs. It had a very long title, and in brief it was known as the Council of National Resistance, an illegal organisation, and which I later recognised in the DB, namely the people from there were the people in the DB. So even a journalist noted that as the people from Knin are not -- a -- are -- now this void has been occupied by the people from the Council of National Resistance. "And the second element was that the unrest and conflicts began in Banija. I don't know who or what caused these conflicts. So the Serbs were accusing the Croatian government, and the Croatian -- the ah -- "THE INTERPRETER: Could you ask him to repeat that? "MR. HARDIN: Could you repeat that? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And the Croatian government was accusing the rebellious Serbs, and Serbia, and the Serbs from Banija were accusing the Croatian government."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] But I remember that Raskovic supported me. He said, `That's the right thing.' And he added: `There is a third element, wishing of the conflict.' So the first two factors, elements, were we and the Croatian government, and he mentioned this third factor, the third element, wishing a conflict. He at that point must have known something more than I did. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But you said the illegal organisation, this Council of National Resistance, were people of -- from the DB. You mean from the DB Serbia or the local DB? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Local people, yes, people who were living in Knin: Dule Orlovic, then Vitas, and others who were there. At a certain point, Dusan Orlovic was the head of DB of Krajina. But I recounted -- I described to you how I've seen that his boss was Jovica Stanisic. It was on the basis of the talk, on that discussion in August 1991. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But, Mr. Babic, let's not get distracted again. You say while you were pursuing peace, other forces were -- other sides were pursuing war. And you mentioned this Council of National Resistance, you mentioned some elements in Banija, and you mentioned a third party whom you -- who Raskovic mentioned. Why can you then say it's Milosevic? How does Milosevic fit into this picture? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, you see, it -- how does he fit in this picture? At the beginning, I didn't know how he fit, but later I was -- it became clear to me that there is a hierarchy and that there's a system: Vitas, Orlovic, Martic, Stanisic. They certainly lead to Milosevic. I think that Stanisic leads to Milosevic, that he wasn't there independently. That's how I see the structure."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] ... Milosevic. A statement on our acceptance of the Cyrus Vance plan and the acceptance of the UN forces. In this discussion, Radovan Karadzic aggressively supported Milosevic and he acted aggressively towards me. And Nikola Koljevic, it was a non-aggressive attitude, but also expressing his support for the position stated by Milosevic. And then Milosevic gave me a sheet of paper, and then I went to another room to write down this statement. And I wrote this statement, approximately on one page. He took, I believe, a pencil, and he said the following -- "MR. HARDIN: `He' meaning who, Milosevic? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Milosevic. Milosevic said the following. He said: `I won't cross it out, but I shall underline what I believe you should leave out.' And then he underlined practically the entire text. What remained was that we -- was the sentence that we accept the peace plan. Well, I, you know, in a subdued tone, I protested. I didn't agree with that. And he responded. He reacted to this by saying, `You're stubborn, stubborn.' He often would say that to me, that I'm stubborn, and he used the English term that I'm a troublemaker.
