And he launched this expression `troublemaker' in May 1991, and it was then that he said that I ought to be killed. Namely, he said that -- he stated, `Some academicians said that you ought to be killed.' "MR. HARDIN: In May 1991? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. When he said that I ought to be killed. But on this occasion, he didn't say it. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But was that a joke? Did he mean it as a joke or did you understand it as a threat? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] A threat. Well, you know, he wanted to conceal it a bit, that it's not his direct threat. You know, he didn't even offer coffee. It was a hostile attitude. "MR. HARDIN: /unclear/in May?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And I think that while I was there and while we were waiting for Jovic to arrive, Branko Kostic was talking to General Krstic over the phone. In fact, Kostic was asking, `Is there anything which has to -- ought to be signed?' I do not remember -- I cannot recollect if there were any other Presidency members present. I remember that he was there because of this scene with the telephone, but the talk, I had the talk with Jovic. "MR. HARDIN: Yes. Now, when you describe the talk with Jovic, I would like you to tell me, as best as you can recall, what he said and what you said. Not necessarily what you thought, but what you and he said. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] First, well, he showed the plan, the text. "MR. HARDIN: `He' meaning Jovic? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Jovic. Jovic showed the text to me. "MR. HARDIN: And `the text' means the Vance Plan? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And I said, `There's nothing new in this.' That is what I said. And he answered. He was arrogant, uppity. He said, `And is there anything new with you?' I said, `No.' And, you know, this is the key impression of that meeting. I don't recollect other things being said. This arrogance and this attitude of him -- of his, this is what remains with me. "MR. HARDIN: So at the time you had this meeting with him, he was already -- it was very -- it was well known by him that you opposed the Vance Plan; is that correct? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. When he -- yes, because he said, `Is there anything new with you?' He meant: Are there any changes in your attitude? I wasn't generally opposed. Generally, I was for, I was accepting the plan. "MR. HARDIN: Yes, just what was said. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. He knew that I had some comments, some observations. It was in this sense that he said, `What's new with you?' I remain behind these comments of mine. So I retain and I stand by these comments of mine. "MR. HARDIN: And what did he reply?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Well, let me just ask a question regarding that and then I'll go back and qualify it. Okay. With that statement I just read, is that true, that that was one of the aspects of contention between what you wanted and what Mr. Milosevic et al. wanted? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't about this. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Hang on. Hang on. Hang on. Hang on just a minute. Hang on. Hang on just now. I'm going to qualify this. What I'm looking at and what I'm reading from is -- I already read the ERN number. No. I'll repeat it for the record. It's 00543360. Okay. And this is an unofficial translation, and it says it's a text of Mr. Milan Babic's response to Slobodan Milosevic, as reproduced in Politika, 12 January 1992. Now, did you write a letter to Slobodan Milosevic on or about that date? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, a letter was written, was drafted by Boro Rasuo, and I did sign a text, and well, he elaborated and put in -- filled it in with different things. "MR. HARDIN: Well, this letter that was written by whoever segment, went out with your signature, did it not? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. "MR. HARDIN: Was that an accurate representation of what you wanted? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] No. "MR. HARDIN: Why did you sign it? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, at the suggestion that the public opinion -- namely, that Slobodan Milosevic created this public opinion. It was -- this was the suggestion by the person who drafted the text, to formulate it in this way for the public. "MR. HARDIN: Yes. Yes. But what do you differ with in this letter? What -- do you recall the letter? I don't have a copy in B/C/S. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] The Vance Plan was not a political plan; it was a security arrangement. "MR. HARDIN: Yes. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And this plan did not encompass, did not incorporate about a quarter of the territory of Krajina in which Serbs lived. And the main opposition and our disagreement was concerning the territory, the size of the territory which should be covered by the peace forces. And I did show to Jovic, to Milosevic, what was not being protected, and they didn't want to talk about it. And then I insisted -- my attitude, I was inflexible on that, on this green line which would divide the forces, separate the forces, and in this way, then it would be possible to protect the entire territory in which Serbs lived. "You know, I couldn't face a situation where a big part of the people would be lacking protection and that I would be then the culprit for this position. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. So let me ask you the question then: When you wrote this letter, is this a political letter or is this how you felt? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Political. "MR. HARDIN: I don't see it here, and I just scanned it -- I don't see it, anything here about the part of the territory of Serbian Krajina which would not be covered under this plan. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] It speaks of this line of separation, speaking of the line of separation and the deployment of the forces which would, in practice, mean the protection of our entire territory."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]... "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Mr. Babic, when I read this letter, there is rhetoric in that which is extremely radical, especially in relation to the Croats that are mentioned here as the `Croatian neo-Nazi aggressors.' And you also speak here of the Vance Plan being realised as the plan, actually allowing the plan of genocide of the Serbs, that you contest that the Krajina is part of Croatia, that you do not want to be disarmed. It sounds from this letter that you are much more radical than Mr. Milosevic himself. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, but these were neither my feelings nor my thoughts. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: But you signed it. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] I was thinking about concrete matters, about the security aspects. Well, the tension and the pressure, a moment of lack of attention. I wasn't more radical. I wasn't more radical than Milosevic, because Milosevic, on the 26th of February, by the Assembly in Borovo Selo, introduced the constitution and the laws of Yugoslavia on the territory of Krajina. There are documents existing about that. And at the time when this letter was published, neither the constitution of Yugoslavia nor the laws of Yugoslavia were in force in Krajina. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Mr. Babic, you gave us, last time, a lot of documents, and in some of the documents were just that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] In -- in practical terms, he occupied on behalf of Yugoslavia, politically, Krajina. Until then, he had the control over the militia, the army. He influenced the economic system via the economy. And on the 26th of February, he also occupied Krajina politically. He took over the power, took over the power. "MR. HARDIN: Yes. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] And these -- these things really pull our attention from what is essential, and it shows me more radical than I was. But in reality, it was different. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. But we've we covered this a little bit some time ago with the October meetings. Is what you just -- I'm sorry. Just please allow me for a couple minutes to see what I'm missing. At the time when you said that he acquired Yugoslav laws into the Krajina in, what, February -- "THE INTERPRETER: 26th. "MR. HARDIN: -- 26th, 1992; correct? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Yes. "MR. HARDIN: Now, at that point, did Croatia, the government of Croatia, have any control over this area in the Krajina? Yes or no. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] No, they didn't. "MR. HARDIN: So the area of the Krajina now became a part of Yugoslavia, as I understand. Is that correct? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Not quite. "MR. HARDIN: What was it then? What was it? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Formally it was a separate area. "MR. HARDIN: Was it part -- "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] In reality, a part of Yugoslavia. "MR. HARDIN: Okay. Now, what did he want? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] On the 9 -- on the 19th of December, we separated from Yugoslavia. "MR. HARDIN: Hang on. Just a minute. We'll talk physical dynamics, geography. On this 26th of February, 1992, according to what you said, what Milosevic caused to happen was that the Serbian Krajina now became part of Yugoslavia. "Now, understanding that politics changed during this period and going all the way back to 1990 and moving up to that date, isn't that the same thing, that the Serbs, represented by you, as the president, wanted was a part of Croatia, being the Serbian part of Croatia, to be divorced from Croatia and then to become part of Yugoslavia or Serbia depending upon what time period we're speaking about? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Not everybody. "MR. HARDIN: Did the government -- the government of the SAO Krajina -- "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Let me ask you -- Mr. Babic, let me ask you. On the 19th -- you said on the 19th December, you decided in the Krajina that you did not want to be part of the Yugoslavia? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] We proclaimed -- we proclaimed ourselves independent, and we stopped being a part of Yugoslavia. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Yes. But at the same time, according to this letter that Mr. Rasuo wrote, you also said, `We don't want to be part of Croatia.' Did you want to be absolutely independent like Monaco sort of? What did you want? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, it was -- it became. The situation became clear. You know, Croatia was already recognised as an independent state by a number of -- it was from the 23rd of December she was recognised as an independent country by Germany and then followed by others. The position then of the international community at the conference on Yugoslavia was -- was clear from the 18th of October, 1990, that there can be no changes of the borders of the former republics of Yugoslavia. So it was clear to everyone that Krajina will have to find its position within Croatia. "Now, in this conflict, which was also an armed conflict and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conflict on an institutional level, there was this radical column, and although the international community had this clear position -- so we had to move gradually. Not Monaco. So we created -- this was created and what we called the Republika Srpska Krajina. It was an institution by which it was possible then with other involved factors, Croatia, the international community, to solve this problem and to solve -- to determine its future position. So -- and it was my conviction and my feeling that this would have to be in a political and territorial community with -- in Croatia. "So from the 18th of October, the second session of that conference when this position was clearly stated, the realistic prospects were these. But you see, we also have to move gradually and also within the public opinion. We had a lot of faith and confidence in these options which were proposed by Milosevic. So we were somewhere in a position in between, between Yugoslavia and Croatia, which became independent. "MR. HARDIN: So you're -- so you're -- okay."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we're moving on -- not very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] So irrespective of what was written in the press, my proposal was that the UN takeover also the civilian administration of Krajina, and that in this way then the international community could slowly, gradually, find this kind of solution. So it was -- but it ought to have been done without big shifts, without great fear in the public, and without vengeance coming from Milosevic. So it was a more muted way of finding a solution within the boundaries of Croatia. "But I already talked about this, that from the moment of the Vance Plan and my proposal for the civilian administration, international civilian administration, an UN protectorate for the Krajina, there was an evil campaign being launched, and it was -- it involved also my aides who were considered to be my close aides, and they diverted the attention from these matters and creating an image of us as radicals and that there was nor strength neither in me personally nor in the institutions of Krajina to come out of this situation more peacefully. So I was really suppressed by this pressure, this atmosphere, this choking atmosphere. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Mr. Babic -- "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] I told you about this, that the municipality of Knin accepted the deployment of the peace forces. It was the first time that the shooting took place in my apartment. I'd like just to depict for you what was the general environment, the general prevailing climate. "MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF: Mr. Babic, I mean, what you tell us now is in absolute contrast to what is written here in this letter. How can you explain that? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I didn't have the strength, the power. I had no other support than these people whom I considered to be the closest to me. I told you that this idea of a UN protectorate for Krajina, these same people didn't want to support it, to back it up. "MR. HARDIN: Mr. Babic -- Mr. Babic, with all due respect, when you say you don't have the power for /unclear/, you have stood three days in the Presidency speaking about the Vance Plan in front of the most powerful people in Yugoslavia. You didn't -- you didn't represent yourself to be a man not afraid to say things or afraid to do things. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Oh, I was less afraid of them than of the angry people, of the angry rank and file. "MR. HARDIN: Yes, but -- "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] How -- how -- how could I -- you know, if somebody said, `Yes, he protected Knin but he didn't protect us,' then you would have revenge. There was the responsibility towards these people whom I represented. I -- I said that this was -- I already mentioned to Madam Hildegard that once, that this was really an existential fear of my very survival."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's finished, then, is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think there is one small piece.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "MR. HARDIN: Frankly, some of the answers you're giving us, especially when it comes to this letter, for example, are in contrast to a lot of things that we have. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Well, I'm talking candidly, sincerely from my heart and from my mind. From the mind and the heart. "MR. HARDIN: Do you have any more you want to ask? Okay. We'll move into a whole different [indiscernible]. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] Do I have to answer, add anything to that? "MR. HARDIN: No. No, you don't have to add anything to that. I just want to advise you, because I have -- I have the feeling, and I don't have to -- and I don't have to be right, nor do I have to be wrong, that you're slanting some of your answers. And like I said, the question is that you have to ask yourself when you decide whether you're going to answer it, just that, whether you have to answer it or not. And when you do, just like what I said, you want to make sure it's as honest as you can make it and as best that your memory can recall. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: [Interpretation] I have to -- but you know, I do that to the best of my abilities, but I have to also tell you what was in my heart, what was in my mind, and what was on my lips."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. We will deal in private session when we come back with what should happen to the exhibits and the like, the Politika decision and the rest of it. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session to deal with these administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The tape itself should have an exhibit number, and attached to it we should obviously have a transcript, when that could be made available, of the relevant section. I think normally we give a Defence number to these documents. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next Defence exhibit number is D57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, perhaps you could help us: When are we likely to be able to have a transcript of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can provide you with a transcript of this section played tomorrow, but if you like, we can also provide you with the entire transcript, in particular, a CD-ROM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us stick with the extract for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We will get it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if the rest becomes necessary, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it would be helpful, if Mr. Milosevic plans to play more of the interview, if he could tell the court deputy, or us, one day in advance, which day and approximate hour he will be playing, and then we could provide you with the transcript of this section in advance. And it would be also easier for you then to follow which sections are left out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The other matters we need to deal with are: The tab number of the order is, I understand, 143 - the Registry have it - not 142. The Politika article, I seem to remember that as being exhibited, but perhaps you could remind me of what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Politika article with the two letters is tab 79 from Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are any other matters relating to that tape, I think we can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to assist you in preparation of your cross-examination, we've decided you can have up to 20 hours cross-examination. We don't encourage you to take that long, but you can if you want. You've had an hour and a half, of course, this morning, playing that tape. We will today sit until 2.00, so you have until then to continue your cross-examination. And would you remember, please, both the accused and the witness, to leave a pause between question and answer, for the interpreters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it is my impression that the time that you are giving me is somewhat shorter than the examination-in-chief took, and as you're indicating the need for making pauses between question and answer, and other forms in which time is wasted, I don't think that you ought to abridge the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time is not abridged. But go on. Let us make a start. We've a lot to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I have played some tapes here, just half, actually, of a large number of tapes that we have from your interviews, Mr. Croatia 61. I could have taken any other tape, but I selected the first tape. Now, did it remind you -- we saw the tape played and we saw on the tape that the lady opposite said to you that what you were saying was in complete contrast with what they had, and you were able to see that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying -- let me remind you. Did you see that a moment ago that even the lady who interviewed you and held the examination-in-chief said that what you were saying was in complete contrast with what they had? I hope you were able to see that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for me to be more specific, I would have to go back into a closed session, and I don't wish to do that. So I'm asking you in open session: Did you remember what you saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interview, I told the truth to the best of my recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you notice that the interviewers, the investigator himself - and this was at the very end of this excerpt from the tape that I played to you - that he presented his impressions that this was in contradiction with what they had, the material they had, and that he had the impression that you were distorting your answers, that they were distorted, slanting your answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can remember, the investigator reminded me that I should speak about the facts that I had seen and heard, and not talk about my feelings and sentiments in my heart and in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, please, this: In view of the fact that the person who was putting the questions to you, and the investigator, was cautioning you about the contrasts that you -- and what you were saying, as opposed to what they had, the material they had, how come that you agreed in the examination-in-chief with everything they said over the past five and a half days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness to answer. He gave his answers. It will be for us to judge the way in which he gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you had made attempts to secure a peaceful and harmonious life for the population of the Krajina with the other inhabitants of Croatia, within the framework of the Republic of Croatia. Is that correct? Is that what you endeavoured to achieve? That's what you say. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that in 1990, the political option in favour of the SAO Krajina was one thing; in 1991, it was something else; and in 1995, again it resembled the option of 1991 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises: 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have seen on this tape, and I think at the examination-in-chief, that in the beginning -- and as we have seen when they are putting questions to you - they keep repeating this, and it's in the transcript - that is, that you, as of 1990, attempted to secure a harmonious life within the framework of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, we wanted the community of municipalities, that is, the SAO Krajina, to achieve political and territorial autonomy within Croatia, and depending on the position of Croatia within Yugoslavia. If it was in a federation, the content of this territorial autonomy would be on a lower level, it would resemble a cultural autonomy; and if Croatia became a confederal republic within Yugoslavia, then the level of autonomy would be higher. That was -- those were the options in 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But we all heard you explaining that from the very beginning, from 1990 onwards, you endeavoured to solve the question or the issue of a harmonious life within the Republic of Croatia. And as far as I was able to see and hear on the tape, your explanations were that what was in your heart and in your mind - you even gestured and pointed to your heart and your head - that this was not what was on your lips, this was not what you were saying. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 -- I explained in great detail how it came about that the SAO Krajina opted for Yugoslavia in 1991. In 1991, I agreed with your conception that the SAO Krajina and the Serbs had the right to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in order to avoid identifying the witness, I will not be more specific here, but I can refer to an article in Politika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how it came about that this article was published? You marked it with number 63. It follows that your statement was not actually yours, that somebody else had made it and that it was published as yours. Is this your explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What article are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The document you marked number 63.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, 63, Mr. Milosevic, is a decree to do with insignia. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to what the witness said when interviewed by the investigator and a representative of the other side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what he himself mentioned as 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. No, I don't think it is 63. I think it's 79. Let the witness see 79. Don't put it on the ELMO. Yes. Now the witness has it. What was the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand how -- what he meant when he said someone else would have signed it, he had not signed it. I don't understand his explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we better go into private session to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Milosevic is referring to tab 130. Is that right? If I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he's referring to tab 143. That's the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I have got the Politika article, which I thought the matter was being referred to, at 79. Mr. Milosevic, could you give us -- tell us again what it is that you're referring to, and we'll find it and make sure that we've all got the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in private session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we're in private session. We need to identify this document that you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to see the document which on the tape we have just seen the witness referred to when he said somebody else would have signed it had he not signed it, and the investigator said this was number 63. I wanted to see this document myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But first of all, what the investigator said is in reference to some other documentation. The document which the Prosecution said was referred to was tab 79, which was a Politika article referring to a reply from the witness to Mr. Milosevic, dated the 12th of January. The original may be somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can assist the parties here, the document Mr. Milosevic is referring to is the document of -- ordering the establishment of the 3rd Operational Zone and signed by this witness. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I remember that this witness had said that if he hadn't signed this document, somebody else would have signed this document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can recall, all the documents concerning the constitution of the Operative Zones were signed by me. This was the idea of setting up a Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But since we are in private session, I can put this question to you now. It is not clear to me whether you, as president, were also the commander of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina. Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the decision on the implementation of the law on the defence of the republic of August 1991, the president of the government or the Prime Minister of the SAO Krajina was to be the civil commander, and the military commander was to have been the commander of the Main Staff of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me precisely. Were you the commander of the Territorial Defence of the Krajina, and as such did you sign a number of documents? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In actual fact, no. Formally and legally, on the basis of the decision on the implementation on the law on the defence of the Krajina, the Prime Minister was to exercise his duties as prescribed by that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the normative part. That is, I signed the formal, legal documents for the constitution of this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not really actually perform your duties. You only did so in a formal and legal sense. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have exercised my duties, but you prevented this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. One thing is not clear to me, then, as we are now discussing the law on Territorial Defence. You explained here that you implemented the law on defence on the territory of the Krajina in such a way that you received the law from my office by fax. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way we implemented this law was that on the basis of the law on the implementation of the legislation of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, the government decided that the law of the Republic of Serbia on defence should be implemented on the territory of the SAO Krajina, and I asked for the text to be sent to me from your office, and I received it in the way I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Judge Kwon then asked you whether you had any other means of obtaining the law, and you explained that the law had been sent to me for my signature, and to expedite matters, you asked for it to be faxed to you so that you wouldn't have to wait for the Official Gazette to come out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. And also let me add: So that you would be informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If the law had been submitted to me for my signature, it could not have been published yet. That's why you received it from my office by fax.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that the Assembly had passed the law and that you had signed it, that the text of the law was in your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's establish some facts, then. The decision passed by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina on the implementation of the law of defence of Serbia on the territory of the Autonomous Province of Krajina, this is the document bearing the number 02172185. This decision was adopted on the 1st of August, 1991, and this is not in dispute. The date is on the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The decision on the implementation of the law on defence of the Republic of Serbia on the territory of the SAO Krajina was adopted on the 1st of August, 1991, and the date is on the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your letter in -- containing the information on the implementation of this law on the territory of the SAO Krajina was written on the 2nd of August following the decision of the 1st of August. And in it, you say that on the basis of the law -- "pursuant to the law on the implementation of the laws of the Republic of Serbia on the territory of the SAO Krajina..." and so on and so forth. So these are incontestable facts. We are talking about the 1st and 2nd of August. Now if you please, look at your exhibit which begins on page 02162249. This is a photocopy of the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 352. Please confirm whether I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's tab 23 of Exhibit 352. The Gazette. The decision -- the decision of the 1st of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Official Gazette should be tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's actually two documents together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milosevic, that's why the Chamber is recommending you to have your associates in the courtroom, to conduct your cross-examination in a better mode. You have to present the exact document to the witness. So consider the matter later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I think it's sufficient for a document to be recognised if I quote the page number, your page number, which is printed on it, and that it isn't hard to find. It's much easier for you than it is for me with all these papers in front of me. But in order to avoid wasting time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on. Have you -- is it the Gazette you want or the decision? Is it the Gazette you want the witness to look at or a decision?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness can look at it, and you can look at it, because you don't need anyone to translate the date for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's see how we go, see if we've got the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, in order not to stray from the main point, we concluded that the law of the SAO of Krajina was passed on the 1st of August. I am now drawing your attention to the fact that this Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia was published on the 27th of July, five days earlier, that is. And at the beginning, in the decree on the promulgation of the law on defence, it can be seen that I signed the decree on the 18th of July. If I signed the decree on the 18th of July and the law was published on the 27th of July, is it sufficiently clear that the witness could have had no need to get this paper, which every lawyer's office in the country sees routinely, to get this through my fax machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the document, the Official Gazette in which the law on defence of the Republic of Serbia was published, I obtained last year and gave it to representatives of the OTP and the investigators to show them what this decision of the 1st of August relates to. So as I have already said during my testimony, I obtained the law by fax, and it is identical with this text, the text that was published in the Official Gazette. So I wanted to show them the Official Gazette to show them the law that we officially implemented in SAO Krajina on the 1st of August, 1991. I didn't know at the time when exactly the Official Gazette had been published, but I learnt that the document was in your office for your signature, and I asked that it be sent to me by fax from your office, as I have already testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to remind you that in answer to a question from Judge Kwon as to whether you had some other way of obtaining the law, you answered that the law was in my office awaiting my signature and that is why you looked for it. However, it is evident that I signed it on the 18th of July, which means that that was not true. And the Official Gazette was in the shops already on the 27th of July, five days before you issued your own law, which is undisputable. So you have said this merely in order to point out that you received such instructions from me, that is, instructions to implement this law. And you know very well that you implemented all the laws of Serbia in those cases when you had no opportunity to write your own. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that is right is that I wanted to get that law in the way I got it because I had been informed that it was in your office. Secondly, I wanted you to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did I caution you, as early as January 1992, that you shouldn't create the impression that you were coordinating your decisions and positions with the leadership of Serbia, and did I inform the citizens of Krajina that they should know that that was not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You wrote something to that effect in your letter. As for the laws, your recommendation was as follows: that it was better for the laws to be copied by us, that is, the laws of Serbia, and to publish them as our own, than to simply proclaim them as being the laws of Serbia in the territory of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does that mean, then, that our position was that you should not implement the laws of Serbia in the territory of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That we should only proclaim them as being our own, that we should simply copy them, and this is what we mostly did later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that when you didn't have time to write out your own, you simply copied the laws of Serbia? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law on the implementation of legal regulations of the Republic of Serbia and SAO Krajina was adopted on the 29th of May, 1991, because in Krajina, the legislation of Croatia had been annulled, with the exception of those laws that were not in contradiction with the regulations of Krajina and the regulations of SFRY. That is why we needed amended laws. We discussed this, and I informed you about this in May, and you said that it was better for us to copy out the laws of Serbia and to publish them as our own than to simply proclaim them, because it wasn't convenient for people to see that these were the laws of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That has nothing to do with reality. My question was: Is it true that I warned the citizens of Krajina that you were not telling the truth when you were saying that you were coordinating your positions with those of the leadership of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already spoken in this Tribunal about the things we had coordinated our views on and things which we held opposite views. I said what I insisted upon and what you insisted upon, and I think that much of my testimony was devoted to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, then: Does it follow from your testimony that I decided about everything? Is that what you are saying? Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming in your testimony that I made all the decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified that you were at the top of the command structures of both the JNA and the parallel structure in Krajina. I testified that your political objective was for all Serbs to live in one state, that the JNA would protect us, that we had the right to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. From your testimony, it follows that everybody listened to what I said except you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about things and time periods and facts when we listened to you and when we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Everybody except you obeyed me. And our conflict was - I don't know how to put it - a minor clash, because I had insisted that a peaceful solution should be adopted, that the Vance plan be adopted, whereas you insisted that the plan be rejected. Is that what we disagreed on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to you with respect to many things, which things I've already said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to those matters later on. But tell me, please: Is it true that I had warned you that rejecting the protection of the peacekeeping forces of the UN would call in question the most substantive interests of the Serbian people? Did I warn you of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You wrote along those lines in the letter published, and a copy of which you sent to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I warn you that rejecting that plan would mean rejecting the possibility to stop further unnecessary loss of human life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that says in your letter too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I tell you that the presence of the United Nations has the sole purpose of preserving peace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is stated in your letter too, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did I say to you that your negative position was an extremely irresponsible act?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is stated in your letter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did I tell you that people should not suffer sacrifices out of conceit of politicians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is stated in your letter too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please: You were explaining, towards the end of this tape - and that also coincides with the final part of your examination-in-chief - that you were doing what you did not intend to do, out of fear for your personal existence. Actually, let me remind you. At the end of the tape that we all viewed, you say that there was a terrible, stifling atmosphere around you, that your associates had different opinions, that the people had different opinions, and that you had to say what you did because you were afraid for your own existence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We feared that we would be left without protection and that Croatia would take revenge on us for the war that you waged, that you would get out of the war and that we would pay the price.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that later too. Can we agree that you explained why you said what you didn't have in mind, that your motive for doing that was fear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand the explanation you gave for saying what you didn't mean, what you didn't want, because you were motivated by fear for your personal existence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that with precision. I don't understand your generalised statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the investigator asked you why you said what you didn't mean, and you said that this was out of fear for your personal existence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the investigator told me to speak only about the facts and not about my feelings and my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We heard that here what you said, so please answer my question. If then you were saying what you didn't mean, and the motive for that was fear, today what you are saying, is that also prompted by the same motive, that of fear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took an oath before this Tribunal that I would tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and I think, and I claim, that the truth is won, and I am still ready to tell the whole truth about everything I need to say before this Tribunal, and not just what were parts of political reactions or partial views. I am ready to tell the whole truth here, about facts, about views, about feelings as well, about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And judging by what you are saying: In an endeavour to have the Vance plan accepted, I favoured war, whereas you, by rejecting the Vance plan, were for peace. Is that what you wanted to explain here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was speaking to the investigators, I was speaking retrospectively about an observation of the overall events. You misled the people of Krajina and the international community that you favoured peace. You imposed the Vance plan on the people of Krajina. You adopted it. You accepted that plan and imposed it on the people of Krajina. But in fact, you also violated it. You did not comply with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think, Mr. May, that there's no need for us to continue in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we agree --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. May, that we should at least make an effort to work in open session as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that it follows from what you are saying that you enjoyed your political role? You say that you knew that you could survive politically only if you said what your surroundings expected of you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I liked my political role, in a sense, and I had to respect public opinion in my political actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were working because of the attraction of the political role, and you were doing things that you did not agree with because of the attraction of your political role; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Occasionally those were the motives, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, no, but there was such a motive too, in certain periods of time and for certain reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you played your political part only because of the power that it implied? For what other motive, if you were doing things you did not agree with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I played my political role because I believed that it could contribute to a better future for the people, for the public good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that for the public good, for the benefit of the public, for you to speak contrary to your convictions, which you are now presenting to us here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak or act in contradiction with my convictions but in line with political pragmatism as to how those convictions could be turned into reality, in what way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as I was able to see, in your explanation you mention that you may have got some things confused, you may have forgotten things. But anyway, on the last tape you even apologise because of such a possibility, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the interviews conducted with me, I said that I said what I could remember but that I had more to say, and at the end of that interview was my statement that I had things to add, things I hadn't said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me, what was the motive of your endeavours? Was it political pragmatism, as you put it, to create the image among the citizens of Krajina that you were coordinating your views with the leadership of Serbia when it comes it your decisions and positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us assume that -- the fact that I sought to explain to the citizens of Krajina that that was not true. That must have had some reason, or maybe it had no reason or no motive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You sought to cheat, to trick the peoples of Krajina, to play around with their destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to play with the citizens of Krajina why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To achieve your plans. And in 1991 they were maximalistic, and later on you revised them. And for the revision of your political plans, you manipulated with public opinion and the people, and the people of Krajina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps that may be a projection of precisely what you were doing with public opinion in Krajina all this time, especially when it is placed in the context of your current explanations of your intentions, as long ago as 1990, to resolve all problems within the framework of the Republic of Croatia. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, we accepted your concept for the solution to the crisis on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, which was the right of all Serbs to remain in one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. MILAN BABIC, we'll come to that later on in due course, but as you mention this, I assume that you know that with the existence of Yugoslavia since 1918, in fact, and that Yugoslavia expressed the interests of all the South Slav peoples, that the Serbs did in fact live in a single state. Not in 1991 or 1992 but since 1918. That is to say since the end of World War I. Is that something you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you ask the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all the Serbs lived in the one state since the end of the First World War in 1918?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the historical facts and that in 1918 a state was set up of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes in such a way that Serbia and Montenegro united and the provisional state of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, which was later on proclaimed to be the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In 1939, within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, the Banovina of Croatia was established, and through the decisions of the National Liberation Movement, the Communist Party, in 1945 the federation was set up of the Yugoslav republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that even in the declaration which you drew up, or whatever the document was called, on unification of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, that it was precisely in that document that you describe the historical course of life in common in a single state, which dates back to 1918 and not 1990 or 1991? Aren't these historical facts that cannot be refuted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept that you advocated and that we accepted in 1990 and 1991 during the disintegration of Yugoslavia was the concept according to which the peoples of Yugoslavia had the right to self-determination up until the point of secession, and you prepared a law along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I do apologise. I did not do that intentionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mueller is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mueller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you mind me asking for a short break now to have a word with my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're just about to break anyway. Let me just see what the question was. Is there a matter -- we'll go into private session if we're not in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now in private session. Mr. Mueller, is there a matter you want to raise with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Not with you, with the client. Not with you, Your Honours; with the client, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, why don't you just go and have a quick word with him here since we've got only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: I would very much like to, but I think what I have to discuss with him under these auspices is not for the public nor for anybody else in this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Two minutes will be absolutely sufficient, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But the point is we're just going out, and we don't want to waste further time. Is it impossible for you to go up to him and say whatever you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: This is quite restricted because I don't speak Serbian. May I make a suggestion, Your Honours, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Let's put it that way: If the client prefers to continue to the termination of today's session, I would agree to that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. C-061, are you happy to go on for another ten minutes or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I do not ask for a break any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're still in private session. Mr. Milosevic, you must take care.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, while we're in private session, Mr. May, while we're in private session, let me ask some more questions which I'm sure you would instruct me to go into private session for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, in view of the fact that quite obviously you presented yourself falsely and hid behind my name during all those years that, as opposed to you, I don't claim that now. I claim what I claimed then. The intercepted conversation, for example, which through you the opposite side is introducing as evidence between me and Radovan Karadzic, for example, dated the 1st of November, 1991, on page 02129072, it was noted there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was noted there that I say to Radovan Karadzic, speaking about you yourself, "What Babic did is dishonourable. It is dishonourable that he said that the Serb government was -- he is lying that Serbia tried to convince him." Is it true that everything you said here you're saying in order to rid yourself of your responsibility and accountability for the serious fate of the Serb people precisely from the Krajina territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to what I said at the press conference in concrete terms on the 30th -- 31st of October, 1991, was that I said that the top echelons of power exerted pressure for us to accept The Hague documents. I didn't mention the government, nor did I mention you personally. One of the journalists asked me which top echelons when we know that there is only one top echelon, and I kept quiet. I didn't dare mention your name, of course. As far as my responsibility and accountability is concerned, I am ready to be subjected to sanctions for my responsibilities. It is not true that I have come here to cast the blame off myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But through your statements, you consciously have accused all Serb leaders in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, to all intents and purposes, and to put the blame on them and rid yourself of the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not accuse anybody. I have just told the truth, the whole truth as far as I know it. I did not wish to shift the blame. I merely presented the facts that I know about. It is not up to me to accuse or to make a judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it not seem to you to be a little grotesque, Mr. Croatia 61 that a man who was in the post of the president of republic and the Prime Minister of the government should describe the events as being -- as an observer, watching through the looking-glass, and not as a participant, as somebody who issued orders and the principal political leader in the territory for a series of years, especially in the critical period that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question? You're making observations, but what's the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me put it. You may wish to hear the answer to it. The question is this: You have given your evidence as though you were not a participant but as merely an observer of these events. Now, if that were put to you, if that suggestion were made to you, what would your answer be to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have made my observations as a participant of the events and as an eyewitness to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this first: When did we meet for the first time? When did we first meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in October. I don't know the exact date, but it was autumn 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. October 1990. And what was the reason for our meeting? Why did you come to see me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but are we in an open session or private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, this is a private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the SDS, Jovan Raskovic, sent me to speak to you or, rather, to sound out the possibility of having the Serbian Democratic Party, whose headquarters were in Knin and of which he was a president, should take part at elections in Serbia. I don't know whether they had been sounded yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any other subject that we discussed apart from that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't. Right. So in October, you asked me what I thought, whether you should take part in the elections or not. And when did we next meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you also said on that occasion, "Where am I?" That is to say, why didn't I come before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go into whether I said, "Here's some coffee," or, "no coffee," or whatever, but if there was nothing else under discussion, when was the next time we met?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next time was when Jovan Raskovic returned from America, and that was in November, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the subject of discussion then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject discussed was for the most part a discussion between you and Mr. Raskovic about assessments of the elections, the electoral results and the concepts for the establishment of the state and society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So we discussed the elections. And when did we next meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And political concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did we next meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next occasion we met was in December.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go further than that. Let's stick to that. We met for the first time and you asked me about the elections in October, and then you say November we discussed the same thing, and then it was December. Now, tell me, is it true that you, on the 17th of February, 1990, that is to say eight months before we ever happened to meet, that you, at the founding Assembly of the SDS held before a rally of 5.000 people in front of the railway station in Knin, that you were elected to the very small leadership, together with the late Raskovic, Opacic and all the rest, (redacted), Cvijeticanin, Stikovac, and the others; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your previous question, I didn't give a full answer. We met not personally, but we had a contact in August through mediation, and that was in fact our first meeting but not face-to-face. We did this through a mediator, Slobodan Vucetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean through a mediator? I learnt that you called for me when I was at a meeting, that you had some problems to lay before me, and once again through an intermediary, I said that you should contact the organs of Yugoslavia because Serbia had nothing to do with what you were about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that you and the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency and the federal secretary for National Defence were there together at a meeting, which meant that it was a common position and that it should be solved by us going to the president of the Presidency, Borisav Jovic, for him to inform us how we would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. MILAN BABIC, do you know that I spent the summer vacationing in Kupari, and I spent ten summers spending my holidays in Kupari, and that particular summer as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that year. I don't know about all the other years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to what you were saying. Is it true that on the 27th of May of that year, that is to say five months before you met me, you were elected as president of the Municipal Assembly of Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And one month later, on the 27th of June of that same year, were you elected president of the communities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 27th of July. It was June. It was two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Two days later. Now, is it true that on the 31st of July you were elected president of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was at the Assembly in Srb where there were 100.000 Serbs from all over Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't at the Assembly, or Sabor, in Srb. It was at a meeting in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was the Sabor Assembly? It was on the 25th of July, 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And so that was before we met. So tell me, please, at that particular rally, the rally of the SDS, was a declaration adopted on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people in Croatia? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Sabor or Assembly in Srb where the declaration on autonomy was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about the leadership of your party? Could it link that autonomy to the option of staying within the SFRY or stepping out from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the declaration it was stated what this kind of autonomy implied, and amongst others, it was precisely defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that at that time it was asserted that if Croatia remained in the SFRY and the Federation, that for the area of Krajina, cultural autonomy would be requested, with the use of the Serb language and Cyrillic script, as well as cultural institutions, the press, radio, television, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the community of municipalities, regional and local self-government. That was the option for the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you envisaged, should the new powers in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croatia insist on a confederal system, that you strove for higher forms of autonomy, political and territorial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that on the 21st of December you accepted the executive president of SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the president of the Presidency, or rather, the Provisional Presidency of the community of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika, I also became the provisional president of the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina, because that Presidency played the role of the Executive Council of SAO Krajina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, for those who do not know this, is it true that the Executive Council in fact means the government, and that it meant in all the republics and at the level of Yugoslavia as well? The Federal Executive Council, the Federal Executive Council of the republics, they were the governments of the republics and the government of the Federation itself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the concepts of the former Yugoslavia, the Executive Council is an executive organ of the Assembly, which implies strict divisions of power in legislation, et cetera. Partially it is a linguistic quirk, but also one of substance. So the government has more power as the executive organ than the Executive Council has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this changed in Yugoslavia and it was no longer called the Executive Council. On the 29th of May, did you in fact become the Prime Minister of the Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that by constitutional law, the statute of SAO Krajina was proclaimed a constitutional law, the Executive Council became the government, and, by the same token, as president of the Executive Council, I became Prime Minister of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All your explanations seem to be that everything that happened, happened alongside your will, by some sort of automation. Do you gain this impression, as the one you're giving me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're dealing with legal procedure, but a political decision to go ahead with anything was needed beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's 2.00 and it's time for us to adjourn. We'll go on tomorrow. There's something I want to deal with in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask one thing of the Chamber as well? It will be of great assistance to us if the accused is able to indicate to the Chamber how much of the remaining --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- 17 1/2 hours of indicated cross-examination time he's likely to use. That time would take us to the end of the three days sitting, roughly, of next week, when there's another five-day break. If he's going to be substantially less than that amount of time, we'd have to get a witness in for next week. If he's likely to want and to use all of that amount of time, then it will not be necessary to get a witness until five days later, for the following week. I suspect there's going to be a change of witness ordering in any event because of the time that's been used, but if the accused - and I recognise it's not an easy exercise - if he could indicate to you, by tomorrow, whether he's likely to use the full time allowed, that would help us in our planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard the request. Perhaps you'd like to think about it. Let me say to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already stated my views, Mr. May. It is my impression -- and I asked you to reassess the time that I will have. Of course I intend to use up all the time that you allot me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We won't go into the matter any further. The Prosecution will have heard that. I say this to the public: that of course this witness is protected, and nothing is to be reported which indicates his identity. We'll adjourn now. 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of November, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
